label: Chronic Pain and Illness
framing: Pain that does not end is its own kind of work, and Scripture does not pretend it away. It gives you a God who knows the body from the inside, and a Paul who asked three times for relief and was answered instead with a grace sufficient for the unrelieved.
cultural: In the ancient world sickness was often read as a verdict, the sign of a hidden sin or a withdrawn favor, and the chronically ill were pushed to the edge of the community. Into that, Jesus touched the leper and dignified the long-suffering woman, refusing the easy arithmetic that made pain a punishment, and the church learned to sit with bodies it could not cure.
historical: Paul carried a thorn in the flesh he never named and never lost. Across the centuries the church built hospitals, Basil of Caesarea founding one in the fourth century, and figures like Joni Eareckson Tada, paralyzed since 1967, have written from inside lifelong limitation rather than from beyond it. The tradition has always known that faith does not require the body to cooperate.
application: Tell God the truth about the pain, including the days you are angry at it, since the Psalms gave you permission long ago. Use the doctors, the medicine, and the pain specialists as gifts and not as a failure of trust, and do not carry the weight alone. Let your church bring meals and prayer and presence, and on the worst days let someone else hold the faith you are too tired to feel.

verses.text: Even if I wanted to boast, I would not be a fool, because I would be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so no one will credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me, or because of these surpassingly great revelations. So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me. But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me.
verses.where: Paul was given what he calls a thorn in the flesh, and he pleaded with the Lord three times to take it away. The answer was not relief but this: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is perfected in weakness. No one knows what the thorn was, and the site's note says perhaps that is a mercy, since people with many kinds of pain have found themselves in it. It is not a rule that God will not heal, and not a reason to refuse a doctor.

verses.text: So I am allotted months of futility, and nights of misery are appointed me. When I lie down I think: ‘When will I get up?’ But the night drags on, and I toss and turn until dawn.
verses.where: Job describes his life as forced labor and his nights as misery. When he lies down he asks when he will get up; the night drags on, and he tosses until dawn. Scripture gives words to the long nights of the body, and God later says Job spoke more rightly of him than his comforters did.

verses.text: And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction grip me. Night pierces my bones, and my gnawing pains never rest.
verses.where: Job says his life is poured out, days of affliction grip him, and at night pain pierces his bones and never rests. He had once wept for others in trouble; now no one helps him. The pain is not only in the body but in being left alone with it.

verses.text: And a woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She had borne much agony under the care of many physicians and had spent all she had, but to no avail. Instead, her condition had only grown worse.
verses.where: A woman has bled for twelve years, has suffered under many doctors, has spent everything she had, and has only grown worse. Mark sets down every part of it: the length, the cost, the failed treatments, the exhaustion of hope. Jesus not only heals her but calls her forward and gives her his word of peace, so that she is seen.

verses.text: One man there had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and realized that he had spent a long time in this condition, He asked him, “Do you want to get well?”
verses.where: Out of a crowd of sick people, Jesus picks one man who has been ill for thirty-eight years and asks whether he wants to get well. The man does not say yes; he explains that he has no one to help him into the water and someone always gets there first. His answer is a lament about being alone. Jesus knew how long he had been there without being told.

verses.text: You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you. And although my illness was a trial to you, you did not despise or reject me. Instead, you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.
verses.where: Paul reminds the Galatians that it was because of an illness that he first preached to them, and that his condition was a trial to them. They did not despise or reject him; they welcomed him as if he were an angel of God. An apostle lived with a body that others had to bear with, and a church received him well.

verses.text: We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time. Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.
verses.where: Paul says the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth, and that believers groan too, waiting for the redemption of their bodies. Having the Spirit does not end the groaning; it gives it a direction. Labor pains are suffering with a promise.

verses.text: He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.
verses.where: Isaiah's Servant is a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, the kind of person others hide their faces from. The word for sorrows covers physical pain as well as grief. Christians have long read this as Christ, who is not a stranger to the body's suffering or to being turned away from.

verses.text: He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak. Even youths grow tired and weary, and young men stumble and fall. But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.
verses.where: The prophet tells weary exiles that the everlasting God does not grow tired, and that he gives strength to the weary. Even the young stumble, but those who wait on the LORD will renew their strength. Some will soar; the last promise, and perhaps the one most needed, is to walk and not faint.

verses.text: I am poured out like water, and all my bones are disjointed. My heart is like wax; it melts away within me. My strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth. You lay me in the dust of death.
verses.where: In the psalm Jesus prayed from the cross, the sufferer describes his body coming apart: poured out like water, bones out of joint, heart like melted wax, strength dried up like a broken pot. Scripture knows the language of a body in pain and puts it in prayer.

links.label: Suffering and the Silence of God

misread.taken: People living with constant pain are sometimes told that their affliction is light and momentary, as if the verse required them to treat their suffering as small, or showed weak faith if it did not feel light.
misread.says: Paul says this of his own sufferings, with beatings, shipwreck and prison behind him, weighed against eternal glory. It is his testimony, not a line to hand to someone else. The site's note says plainly that to a person in fresh pain, being told it is only light and momentary is not comfort but a wound, and that the verse does not call suffering good. If your suffering does not feel light, you are not failing; many of the psalms are cries from people for whom it did not feel light either.
misread.text: For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.

whole: If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust, a friend, a pastor or a doctor; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Pain that does not end is its own kind of work. People who live with it describe the planning around it, the good days and bad days that no one else can predict, the appointments and treatments that help a little or not at all, the sleep it steals, and the slow loss of things they used to do. Often it cannot be seen, and others stop asking. Some are told it must be in their head, or that they would be healed if they had more faith, and they carry that too.

Scripture does not pretend pain away. Job described nights of tossing until dawn and pain that never rests. The woman in Mark had suffered twelve years and spent everything on doctors. The man at the pool had waited thirty-eight years with no one to help him. Paul lived with a thorn he prayed three times to be rid of, and he first preached to the Galatians because of an illness. The Bible refuses to treat any of them as people of weak faith. It says plainly that the whole creation groans, and believers with it, as they wait for the redemption of the body. Pain belongs to a world that is not yet healed.

Wisdom for the long haul looks different from wisdom for a crisis. It means good medical care, kept up over years, and honesty with doctors about what helps and what does not. It means pacing: learning what a day can hold and accepting that some days hold less. It means letting the church be what the Galatians were to Paul, people who receive a person whose body is a trial to them rather than turning away. It means praying for healing without making faith hang on the answer, as Paul did. And it means bringing the pain itself to God in the honest language of Job and the psalms, which God kept in his book. Grace that is sufficient is often given one day at a time, like manna.

The Christian hope here is not that pain will always be explained, or always removed in this life. It is that Christ is a man of sorrows who knows the body's suffering from the inside, that his power is somehow made perfect in weakness, and that the groaning of creation is the groaning of labor, not of death. The day is coming when the body itself will be redeemed. Until then, your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body, and the promise for the long middle stretch is the one at the end of Isaiah 40: to walk and not faint.
deep.sit: What would it look like to let one person carry a little of this with you this month, and who would that be?

prayer.lead: David calls himself poor and needy and asks God to hear him in the day of trouble. Pray it slowly on a bad day, as someone who has a right to be heard.
prayer.text: Incline Your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul, for I am godly. You are my God; save Your servant who trusts in You. Be merciful to me, O Lord, for I call to You all day long. Bring joy to Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul. For You, O Lord, are kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You. Hear my prayer, O LORD, and attend to my plea for mercy. In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me.

careLines.text: If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith.
Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body.
If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
